Who pays, who bears the risk, who decides, and when? Virginia Commissioner Jehmal Hudson makes a forceful case that serving large-load growth requires credible commitments, earlier coordination, and ratepayer protections built into investment decisions.
Judge Jehmal T. Hudson, commissioner of the Virginia State Corporation Commission and incoming president of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC).
Good afternoon. Thank you to POWER Magazine for inviting me to join you today.
It is a pleasure to be with so many people thinking seriously about one of the most consequential issues facing the electric industry: how we meet extraordinary new demand while maintaining the affordability, reliability, and financial discipline customers expect from the electric system.
I come to this conversation wearing two hats. First, I serve as a Commissioner of the Virginia State Corporation Commission. Virginia gives us an important vantage point because we are confronting, in real time, many of the questions other states may increasingly face as large loads seek to connect to the grid.
Second, later this year, I will have the privilege of serving as President of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners.
From those perspectives, I believe the regulatory conversation is evolving. We are moving from project-by-project reaction toward system-level strategy.
Data center growth is no longer simply a utility-service question or a single interconnection proceeding. At sufficient scale, it touches utility commissions, state energy offices, economic development agencies, consumer advocates, local governments, utilities, communities, large-load customers, RTOs, and federal regulators.
Increasingly, states must think about large-load growth as a whole-of-government and whole-of-system challenge. And I believe four questions should guide that work:
Who pays? Who bears the risk? Who decides? And increasingly: When do we decide?
From Individual Projects to System-Level Strategy
For much of the electric industry’s history, regulators planned around relatively predictable patterns of demand. Today, the scale, speed, and concentration of proposed load growth are challenging those assumptions.
A single customer may seek hundreds of megawatts. Multiple customers may seek service in the same geographic area. Generation, transmission, substations, and distribution facilities may all be implicated.
That means a decision involving one customer can have consequences across the entire system. So we need to look beyond individual projects and ask what all of this means collectively for the electric system and existing customers.
If we underestimate demand, we can face reliability problems, insufficient generation, delayed economic development, and inadequate infrastructure. But if we overestimate demand, we can construct billions of dollars of infrastructure that someone still has to pay for.
That brings us to one of the hardest questions facing regulators: What demand is real?
The electric system cannot be planned around press releases. We cannot simply add every requested megawatt together and assume all of it will appear exactly when requested.
Regulators increasingly must look not only at the megawatts requested, but at the certainty behind those megawatts. Does the customer control the site? Are permits progressing? Has financing been secured? When will the load materialize? How quickly will it ramp? And what happens if the project is delayed, downsized, or never built?
If utilities build too far ahead of demand, existing customers may become exposed to underutilized assets and stranded costs. If utilities build too slowly, legitimate projects may not receive service when needed.
So the answer cannot be to build everything requested. And the answer cannot simply be to say no. The answer is better information and greater certainty.
The more confidence we have in the demand forecast, the more confidently we can make decisions about generation, transmission, distribution, resource adequacy, and cost responsibility.
Tariff Design Is Risk Design
That brings me to who pays and who bears the risk. Traditionally, tariff design has been viewed primarily as a mechanism for determining how utility costs are recovered.
With very large loads, regulators increasingly must think about it more broadly. Tariff design is also risk design.
Minimum usage commitments, contract duration, collateral, exit fees, construction contributions, and separate rate classes can all help determine who bears the risk before infrastructure is constructed.
Virginia provides a concrete example. In November 2025, the Virginia State Corporation Commission approved a new rate class for Dominion Energy Virginia’s largest customers.
Beginning January 1, 2027, the GS-5 class will apply to customers with measured or contracted demand of 25 megawatts or greater on a contiguous site and a measured or expected load factor of at least 75%.
But creating a separate class was only part of the decision. The Commission also established stronger financial commitments associated with service to those customers.
Certain customers will be required to pay a minimum of 85% of contracted distribution and transmission demand and 60% of generation demand, among other requirements.
Why does that matter? Because infrastructure decisions are made based on anticipated demand.
If a utility constructs infrastructure based on a customer’s representation that it needs a certain amount of capacity, and that demand does not materialize, the cost does not disappear. Someone pays.
The regulatory question is whether that risk should automatically migrate to other customers.
Virginia is also examining transmission cost responsibility. In another proceeding, the Commission directed Dominion to require mandatory contributions in aid of construction for defined transmission facilities necessary to directly connect certain new large-load facilities.
The Commission also left open whether some upstream transmission costs might warrant different treatment.
These are difficult questions because electric infrastructure can create broader system benefits. So cost causation cannot be the end of the analysis.
We also must ask: Who caused the cost? Who benefits? Who bears the risk? And therefore, who should pay?
Match Physical Commitments With Financial Commitments
That leads to a principle I believe deserves greater attention: Physical commitments should increasingly be matched by financial commitments.
If the electric system is being asked to make a substantial physical commitment to serve a customer, what financial commitment should appropriately accompany that request?
If hundreds of millions—or potentially billions—of dollars are invested based on anticipated demand, what assurance exists that the customer will remain financially responsible for an appropriate portion of that commitment?
The answer will differ across jurisdictions. But the scale of the financial commitment should bear some reasonable relationship to the scale of the system commitment being requested.
And there is an important connection here to speed to power. Financial discipline does not necessarily slow development.
Greater financial certainty can produce greater planning certainty. That can allow utilities and regulators to distinguish serious projects from speculative demand and support faster infrastructure decisions for projects truly ready to proceed.
So customer protection and speed to power do not have to compete. Properly designed, they can reinforce one another.
Coordination Before Decisions Harden
That brings me to who decides—and when. Large-load development can involve commissions, utilities, economic development agencies, state energy offices, local governments, communities, RTOs, FERC, and others.
The challenge is that these institutions often make decisions on different timelines. A site may be selected before the utility fully understands its infrastructure implications. Economic development incentives may be discussed before total system costs are known. A utility may begin planning before the commission has determined the appropriate tariff structure.
By the time all of the institutions are talking to one another, important decisions may already have hardened. That is why early coordination matters.
Earlier information-sharing about potential sites, likely demand, infrastructure constraints, resource needs, community concerns, and development timelines can reduce delay, rework, stranded-investment risk, and public opposition.
But coordination does not mean collapsing institutional responsibilities. State commissions must preserve their independent and adjudicatory roles. FERC has its responsibilities. RTOs have theirs. Local governments and state policymakers have theirs.
Coordination should strengthen jurisdiction—not erase it. That is why regulatory sequencing will become increasingly important.
It is not simply who makes the decision. It is whether the right information reaches the right institution at the right time.
Ratepayer Protection and Public Trust
This brings me to ratepayer protection. For regulators, the important question is how that principle translates into actual commission practice.
To me, that means asking hard questions before costs become embedded in rates. What infrastructure is actually necessary? What assumptions support the forecast? Which investments primarily serve the new customer? Which investments provide broader system benefits? What financial protections exist? What happens if demand does not materialize? And what portion of that risk should appropriately be borne by the broader customer base?
Those questions are much easier to address before infrastructure is constructed than afterward. That is why I think about ratepayer protection this way:
Ratepayer protection is not simply about allocating costs after they have been incurred. It is about allocating risk before the investment decision is made.
And that connects directly to public trust. Data center growth can bring significant economic benefits.
But communities are also asking questions about electricity rates, reliability, water, land use, infrastructure, and whether the costs and benefits of growth are being shared fairly.
Regulators maintain trust not by promising that every decision will satisfy every stakeholder, but by demonstrating that the process is disciplined, transparent, and fair. That means explaining our reasoning and being clear about who is bearing which costs and risks.
It means listening to utilities and large customers—but also existing customers, consumer advocates, and communities. If the public believes that benefits are private while risks are socialized, confidence in the system will erode.
Durable growth therefore requires more than infrastructure. It requires public confidence in the decisions that allow that infrastructure to be built.
NARUC: Moving From Diagnosis to Solutions
This brings me to my incoming NARUC presidency. Our three-year theme is “Uniting Regulators, Harmonizing Impact.” For the coming year, my subtheme is “Getting It Right Together.”
And I believe we are reaching an important point in the large-load conversation. We have spent considerable time diagnosing the challenge. Now we need to move increasingly toward solutions.
Work across NARUC, NCEP, and the states is helping identify a growing toolbox: early interagency coordination, improved load forecasting, shared information, large-load interconnection policies, large-load tariffs, financial commitments, and greater alignment around economic-development and infrastructure goals.
No single approach will work everywhere. Virginia does not have every answer. Neither does another state, FERC, an RTO, a utility, or a hyperscaler. But states should not have to learn in isolation.
One commission may be examining minimum demand commitments. Another may be developing a separate tariff. Another may be addressing collateral or exit fees. Another may be confronting transmission cost allocation. Another may be experimenting with flexible service.
We should compare those approaches, understand what is working, and identify principles that can travel across state lines without assuming every state must reach the same outcome.
That is what Getting It Right Together means. It does not mean getting it identical together. It means learning together.
And large-load growth intersects with each of my six priorities for NARUC: affordability; the need for new generation; resource adequacy; balancing costs as utilities evolve; maintaining reliability; and investment needs and ratepayer pressures.
This is not simply a data-center issue. It is a test of whether our regulatory institutions can adapt to rapid economic and technological change while maintaining affordability, reliability, financial discipline, and public trust.
Conclusion
So let me close where I began. We are moving from project-by-project reaction toward system-level strategy. And four questions should guide us.
Who pays? Cost allocation should reflect both cost causation and broader system benefits.
Who bears the risk? Extraordinary or uncertain demand should not automatically transfer extraordinary risk to customers who did not create it.
Who decides? We need coordination among commissions, state policymakers, FERC, RTOs, utilities, local governments, customers, and communities while respecting institutional responsibilities.
And: When do we decide? Because early coordination and regulatory sequencing can help us identify risks before sites are locked in, infrastructure is committed, and costs become difficult to unwind.
The demand opportunity is real. The economic opportunity is real. The infrastructure challenge is real. And the risks are real.
Our job as regulators is not to stop growth. It is to create the conditions for durable growth—growth supported by better information, credible commitments, fair cost allocation, reliable infrastructure, and public confidence.
We need to reduce uncertainty without reducing scrutiny. We need to accelerate infrastructure without accelerating the transfer of risk to customers.
And the ultimate question is not simply whether we can power the next data center. It is whether we can build an electric system capable of supporting the next era of American economic growth while remaining affordable, reliable, financially sustainable, and worthy of the public’s trust.
Growth is coming. Our responsibility is to accommodate it responsibly. To understand who pays. Who bears the risk. Who decides. And when those decisions need to be made.
That is the regulatory challenge. That is the opportunity before the states. And that is what I mean when I say: Getting It Right Together.
Thank you.
—Judge Jehmal T. Hudson is serving his second term as a commissioner of the Virginia State Corporation Commission. He is first vice president and incoming president of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC). Before joining the Commission, he served as vice president of government affairs at the National Hydropower Association and spent 10 years at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, including as director of government affairs. He also serves on the Electric Power Research Institute’s Advisory Council.

The Takeda spinout showed that a high dose of solengepras can shorten the periods during which difficult Parkinson’s disease symptoms like involuntary movements and sleepiness.
Takeda neuroscience spinout Cerevance will head to the FDA to discuss an approval path for the Parkinson’s disease therapy solengepras after the drug reduced the period of time in which standard drugs wear off and symptoms return during a late-stage clinical trial.
A high 150-mg dose of solengepras improved average daily “off time” by 0.61 hours as compared to placebo at week 12, meeting the main goal of the Phase 3 ARISE trial. This benefit showed up as early as the second week. Conversely, the therapy also increased “on time” without difficult symptoms like dyskinesia—the hallmark involuntary, erratic movements associated with Parkinson’s. This was a key secondary endpoint of the trial.
Cerevance also noted improvements in daytime sleepiness and quality of life, which “point to broad motor and non-motor benefit,” according to a Wednesday press release . The data were presented at the 2026 International Congress of Parkinson’s Disease and Movement Disorders in Seoul, Korea.
The ARISE study examined two solengepras doses as an adjunct treatment in 341 patients with Parkinson’s who experience motor fluctuations with standard-of-care levodopa and other medications. At baseline, patients on average experienced 5.65 hours of off time daily. That number dropped by 1.56 hours in patients receiving the 150-mg dose, versus a 0.95-hour drop in the placebo group. Participants in the higher-dose group also showed statistically significant motor improvements, additional secondary endpoints of the trial. Cerevance did not report efficacy data for the lower 75-mg dose.
The privately held company will now head to the FDA to discuss a regulatory path for solengepras.

As for safety, Cerevance said that solengepras was generally well tolerated. No serious adverse events were reported in the solengepras 150-mg dose group, compared with a rate of 1.8% for the 75-mg arm and 0.9% for placebo, and overall discontinuation rate due to adverse events across all arms of the trial, including placebo, was 3.5%. The most commonly reported safety events were headache and urinary tract infection.
Solengepras targets the GPR6 receptor to improve motor and non-motor function without altering dopamine levels or signaling as do standard Parkinson’s therapies, which do not address the underlying cause of the disease and often wear off as the brain’s ability to store dopamine continues to fade. Levodopa specifically can cause dyskinesia over time, leading to increases in off time. Cerevance reported dyskinesia in 4.4% of patients receiving the high dose of solengepras compared to 1.8% for placebo.
Cerevance is one of a few companies working to improve treatment options for patients with Parkinson’s. Late last month, AbbVie received approval for tavapadon , which is to be marketed as Juvmo. The drug, which is the first selective D1/D5 receptor agonist to become available in the U.S., came from the $8.7 billion takeout of Cerevel in December 2023.
But drug development in the space has been tough, with many failed attempts such as Biogen and Denali’s BIIB122. The therapy failed to slow disease progression during a Phase 2b trial and was discontinued earlier this year .
Other biotechs in the game include Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Eli Lilly’s Ventyx Therapeutics and Insilico Medicine.

Zim Integrated Shipping Services raised its full-year 2026 earnings guidance Oct. 6, citing continued strong market demand and favorable freight-rate momentum.
The revised forecast increases the midpoint of its adjusted operating earnings outlook by 72% from guidance issued in August.
The Israeli container carrier (NYSE: ZIM ) now expects adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2.7 billion to $3 billion, up from its previous range of $2 billion to $2.4 billion. Adjusted earnings before interest and taxes are projected at $1.4 billion to $1.7 billion, compared with the earlier forecast of $700 million to $1.1 billion.
At the midpoint, the new outlook puts adjusted EBITDA at $2.85 billion, an increase of $650 million, or approximately 30%. The adjusted EBIT midpoint rises to $1.55 billion from $900 million. Both comparisons are against the company’s Aug. 19 forecast for the year ending Dec. 31.
Zim attributed the upgrade to “continued strong market demand and favorable momentum in freight rates.” The announcement did not provide updated cargo-volume projections or quantify how much of the increase reflected rates rather than shipment demand.
The higher outlook comes as Zim awaits completion of its pending acquisition by Hapag-Lloyd. In its announcement, the company identified uncertainty surrounding the transaction, geopolitical instability and fluctuations in freight rates, vessel supply and shipping demand among factors that could cause actual results to differ from its projections.
Zim’s guidance uses adjusted financial measures rather than results prepared under International Financial Reporting Standards. The company cautioned that adjusted EBITDA excludes debt-service requirements and capital expenditures and should not be treated as a measure of cash available for its use.

YUMA PROVING GROUND, Ariz. — After the joint force and its federal agency partners spent almost a month in the near-vacant desert training to defeat drones coming over the US-Mexico border, military officials have opted to hold their next large-scale counter-drone dri ll in a very different setting: a bustling city with oodles of people and buildings.
“Homeland defense is not about protecting from outside; it’s also protecting inside. We could do one without taking care of the other, and that’s not the right answer,” Brig. Gen. Jason Rueschhoff, operations director of US Northern Command , told reporters on Sept. 24 in Yuma during Falcon Peak 26.2 — the fourth iteration of the exercise.
“The big things for us to be focused on will be collateral damage issues,” he said.
Falcon Peak is run by NORTHCOM, and the most recent exercise in September at Yuma marked the first time officials from the command, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Army-led Joint Interagency Task Force (JIATF) 401 and the Department of Homeland Security all came together for the exercise. Together, they tested ways to neutralize drone threats in the open desert — whether through electronic means or by blasting them out of the air — and learned how the heat, wind and sand can wreak havoc on different systems, as Breaking Defense previously reported .
But like Rueschhoff, Marine Col. Scott Humr said he expects the next edition, scheduled for about a year from now, to be more complicated, considering the physical, operational and legal challenges that come with operating in and around populated civilian areas.
In regards to physical barriers, dense buildings, electronic “congestion” and other physical obstacles create signal interference and “block the line-of-sight required for conventional radars and cameras,” Humr , the deputy director of science and technology for JIATF 401 , said.
“Legally and operationally, defending urban areas in the homeland requires navigating strict domestic policies, complex jurisdictional boundaries and heightened collateral-damage concerns that are not present on an open test range,” he said.
Humr noted that JIATF 401’s “primary takeaway” going from the recent Falcon Peak to the next one will be taking a “highly coordinated” interagency approach, especially working closely with DHS and the Federal Aviation Administration.
In the past, coordinating with such agencies hasn’t been so seamless. For example, in February the FAA suddenly and mysteriously shut down the airspace around the busy El Paso, Texas airport. It was later discovered that the emergency was related to a miscommunication between federal agencies about the use of a counter-drone laser by Customs and Border Patrol, on loan from the Army.
Since then though, military officials have emphasized close coordination with the FAA, culminating in a joint agreement for a laser system to protect the southern border. Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, JIATF 401’s commanding general, also told reporters during Falcon Peak that the task force and the military writ large continues to coordinate testing with the FAA.
But Rueschhoff and Humr said perhaps the highest priority, and a key challenge, will be learning how to protect any civilian population from any collateral damage. In the desert, there are relatively few issues with using a shotgun to simply blast a quadcopter out of the sky, but Humr said that for an urban environment, the Pentagon and task force will focus on using low-collateral and non-kinetic options to make congested environments as safe as possible.

Two logistics and distribution companies have agreed to pay a combined $2 million to resolve federal employment discrimination cases involving allegations that women and other applicants were denied jobs based on sex, race or national origin.
The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission announced Monday that Birchstone Management, a Dallas-based warehousing and logistics management company, agreed to pay $500,000 after an investigation found the company rejected qualified women seeking pallet repair jobs.
The settlement comes less than two weeks after the EEOC announced Denver-based Mile Hi Companies would pay $1.5 million to resolve a federal lawsuit alleging discriminatory hiring practices involving Black, female and Afghan applicants.
EEOC says Birchstone rejected women for pallet repair jobs
The EEOC said its investigation found that Birchstone Management turned away a qualified woman who applied for a pallet repairer position at the company’s Spokane Valley, Washington, location solely because of her sex.
The agency said the practice extended beyond one applicant and location. Since at least May 2020, Birchstone allegedly rejected other qualified female applicants for pallet repair jobs in Spokane Valley; Amarillo and Houston, Texas; Lakewood, Washington; and Las Vegas.
Instead, according to the EEOC, Birchstone hired men with similar or fewer qualifications or continued looking for male applicants.
“I showed up ready to demonstrate my ability to do the job, only to be told that the company only hires men,” the applicant who filed the charge said in the EEOC announcement. “I hope this case helps employers stop labeling jobs as ‘women’s work’ or ‘men’s work.’”
Birchstone agreed to provide $55,000 to the woman and establish a $445,000 settlement fund for other affected applicants.
The agreement resulted from the EEOC’s pre-litigation conciliation process rather than a lawsuit.
Along with monetary relief, Birchstone must revise its hiring and recruitment policies, provide training to personnel involved in hiring at several locations, audit its employment recordkeeping annually and report to the EEOC for two years.
Mile Hi Foods settles EEOC lawsuit for $1.5M
The Birchstone settlement follows a Sept. 25 announcement that Mile Hi Companies , a Denver-based distributor of food and paper products, agreed to pay $1.5 million to settle an EEOC lawsuit filed in 2024.
The allegations in that case extended beyond sex discrimination.
The EEOC alleged Mile Hi denied employment opportunities to Black, female and Afghan applicants beginning in 2015.
According to the agency’s lawsuit, the company’s CEO directed employees to limit the percentage of Black applicants hired, not hire women for warehouse positions and stop hiring Afghan applicants for bakery jobs.
When the company’s human resources manager opposed those directives, the EEOC alleged Mile Hi retaliated against her by harassing and eventually firing her.
The EEOC filed the lawsuit in September 2024 after the agency said efforts to reach a settlement through its administrative conciliation process were unsuccessful.
Under a three-year consent decree, Mile Hi must provide monetary relief to the former HR manager and affected applicants. The company also must review its employment policies, train employees and managers on anti-discrimination laws, maintain applicant records and periodically report its compliance efforts to the EEOC.
Women remain underrepresented in transportation
The cases come as the transportation industry continues to grapple with attracting and retaining women in jobs historically dominated by men.
A 2024 American Transportation Research Institute study found significant barriers for women entering and remaining in trucking, ranging from negative stereotypes and company culture to inadequate facilities and gender harassment.
ATRI surveyed nearly 1,500 current and former truck drivers and also conducted interviews and focus groups with drivers, motor carriers and truck-driving schools. Women accounted for roughly half of the driver survey respondents.
Women reported experiencing 11 of 12 problems examined by researchers more frequently than men. About 17% of female respondents said they encountered harassment or discrimination daily, roughly twice the rate reported by male drivers.
Why it matters: The settlements highlight persistent barriers for women seeking jobs in traditionally male-dominated freight and logistics occupations, an issue also documented in transportation industry research.

Packaged goods supply chains are full of examples of exception requests, like when a retailer asks for a custom pack configuration, a key account needs a special label, or a shipment gets rerouted on short notice to hit a delivery window. Those kinds of exceptions aren’t necessarily problems on their own. Exception handling can look like good customer service. But on Oct. 15, FreightWaves and G3 Logistics are asking what happens when you stop counting those requests one at a time and start adding them up.
That’s the topic of The Hidden Cost-to-Serve in Packaged Goods: Managing Rework, Specialized Handling, and Operational Exceptions , a free webinar that will dig into the repack jobs, relabeling work, retailer-specific requirements, and expedited changes that accumulate inside packaged goods networks until they’re no longer exceptions at all. Without visibility into what those exceptions cost, they can be devastating to margins over time.
G3 Logistics brings transportation, warehousing, and supply chain expertise to a common packaged goods challenge: customer requests that add work beyond the standard flow. A package change, relabeling request, or tighter delivery window can affect handling, schedules, inventory, and capacity across multiple teams. Seeing those effects together helps leaders understand hidden costs and make more intentional service decisions.
Jerry Knight, G3’s Senior Director of Global Logistics, and Nicole Ostertag, Head of Solutions, will explore when a reasonable exception becomes a recurring operating cost—and what should change when it does.
A one-off retailer packaging request for a promotion can look like a manageable commercial accommodation, until the extra handling, line interruptions, inventory segregation, and tighter turnaround windows it requires start showing up in every subsequent run for that account. Rework that begins as occasional recovery work (such as relabeling, repacking, or fixing damaged product) can quietly become a standing part of daily operations, its cost buried inside standard labor instead of tracked anywhere finance or ops can see it. The accounts that matter most commercially are often the ones creating the most operational drag, including frequent small runs, narrow delivery windows, or constant manual workarounds to hit a service level that is now taken for granted.
The discussion is structured as a working session for supply chain leaders to compare notes on where these costs show up first, which ones are easy to see on a P&L, which stay buried in additional touches and lost throughput, and who in the organization actually owns the decision to say yes to a request. The webinar is designed to give you a sharper read on how to measure hidden costs at the customer, SKU or channel level, where other companies have had success clawing back margin through order rules, packaging redesign, customer segmentation or clearer exception pricing, and a clearer sense of which functions need to be in the same room to make any of it stick.
Hidden costs rarely announce themselves as a logistics problem or a warehouse problem. They sit at the intersection of commercial commitments, packaging decisions, and operational execution. Leaders can address them by making exceptions visible before workarounds become part of daily operations.
The webinar is free to attend. If you’re responsible for packaging, operations, planning, or customer service in a packaged goods supply chain, you’ll want to be in the room before the hidden costs in your own network get any harder to see.

Core at the Los Azules copper project in Argentina, where TNR Gold has a royalty. Credit: McEwen
Posted By: Colin McClelland October 7, 2026
Altius Minerals (TSX: ALS) has made an unsolicited, non-binding proposal to acquire the 87% of TNR Gold (TSXV: TNR; US-OTC: TRRXF) it doesn’t already own, a move that would give it control of royalties over two major Argentine copper and lithium projects.
Vancouver-based TNR hasn’t disclosed the offer price or other financial terms. At TNR’s Wednesday morning share price of 32¢, the company is valued at about $78 million and Altius’ proposed purchase of the remaining shares would be worth roughly $68 million before any takeover premium.
TNR has entered into an exclusivity arrangement with Altius after a special committee of independent directors reviewed the proposal, TNR said Wednesday . The committee is continuing to assess the approach and no definitive transaction has been agreed. Altius had signalled its interest in TNR’s royalty portfolio when it first invested for 9.9% of the company in May.
“The TNR royalty portfolio includes exposure to major copper and lithium deposits,” Altius said at the time. “We look forward to working constructively with the TNR team as its royalty portfolio and business continues to advance and mature.”
Shareholder dispute
The approach comes amid a months-long shareholder dispute at TNR involving New York-based Eucalyptus Resources Opportunities Fund, which has sought changes to the company’s board and criticized Altius’ initial investment as dilutive. On Monday, TNR and Eucalyptus agreed to discontinue a court petition and give the existing board time to complete its strategic review.
TNR shares gained 8.3% in Toronto on Wednesday morning after closing Tuesday at 30¢. They’ve traded between 9¢ and 36.5¢ over the past year. The company has a market capitalization of $80.9 million. Altius has been steadily building its position in TNR this year. Its subsidiary invested $4.2 million in May for 23.5 million shares at 17.75¢ each.
The investment also gave Altius a right of first offer over TNR’s interests in royalties covering the Mariana lithium project and Los Azules copper project in Argentina. Altius said at the time the investment fit its strategy of taking minority stakes in companies holding royalties over large mineral deposits.
Altius increased its position in July by buying another 7.4 million shares at 23¢ each for about $1.7 million. That lifted its holding to 30.9 million shares, or about 13%. Based on that stake, TNR has about 244 million shares outstanding.
Royalty portfolio
TNR’s main assets include a 0.4% net smelter return royalty on McEwen’s (TSX, NYSE: MUX) Los Azules project in San Juan province, Argentina, although 0.04% is held on behalf of another shareholder.
Los Azules is one of Argentina’s largest undeveloped copper projects. A 2025 feasibility study outlined proven and probable reserves containing 10.2 billion lb. copper and average production of about 205,000 tonnes of copper cathode annually during its first five years.
TNR also holds a 1.5% net smelter return royalty on Ganfeng Lithium’s Mariana project in Argentina, including a 0.15% interest held for another shareholder. Ganfeng can repurchase 1% of the royalty for $1 million, which would leave TNR with a 0.45% interest.
Mariana began producing lithium chloride last year and made its first export in February.
TNR also has a 7% net profits royalty over the Batidero I and II properties at the Josemaria project being advanced by Lundin Mining (TSX: LUN) and BHP (NYSE, LSE, ASX: BHP), and owns 90% of the Shotgun gold project in Alaska.
In addition to Eucalyptus’ criticism of Altius’ original investment in April, it also objected to the associated voting agreement and rights over TNR’s royalties. TNR and Eucalyptus subsequently clashed over the company’s annual meeting and the ownership and voting of shares.
TNR has scheduled its annual and special shareholder meeting for Dec. 8.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI, the first electric hot hatch to bear the iconic GTI badge.
Volkswagen launches ID. Polo GTI pre-orders
To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen is “starting a new chapter” with the first all-electric GTI model.
Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI on Wednesday, starting at 39,995 euros, or about $45,000.
The first all-electric model to wear the GTI badge, “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW said.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 222 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.
The electric hot hatch looks and feels like “a quintessential GTI” with the typical honeycomb pattern, the red stripe up front, and standard 19″ alloy wheels.
Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI electric hot hatch (Source: Volkswagen)
It may not be the fastest, but Volkswagen promises the ID. Polo is a proper hot hatch that’s fun to drive.
A fun electric hot hatch
Volkswagen developed a new “GTI” driving profile that unlocks the vehicle’s full potential. At the push of a button on the steering wheel, the electric drive, steering, and suspension will automatically adjust to maximize performance and response.
An electronically controlled front axle transverse differential lock precisely distributes power to the front wheels, making it easier to corner and maneuver.
Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI interior (Source: Volkswagen)
Inside, the interior is blacked out with sporty red elements. The electric hot hatch features a new GTI sports steering wheel and premium sports seats.
Based on VW’s new cabin design, the ID. Polo GTI features a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit and 12.9″ infotainment display.
Like the standard model, the ID. Polo GTI has a new “Retro Display” that transforms the instrument display and infotainment screen to resemble that of the first-generation Golf. Even the music sounds like it’s from the ’80s, as if it were a cassette.
The ID. Polo GTI uses the same 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery as the standard model, which provides a WLTP driving range of up to 431 km (267 miles).
With DC fast charging up to 105 kW, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 24 minutes.
Measuring 4,096 mm long, 1,816 mm wide, and 1,514 mm tall, with a 2,599 mm wheelbase, the ID. Polo GTI is about the size of the gas-powered VW Polo.
Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI (Source: Volkswagen)

Vizsla Copper's Palmer copper-zinc project in southeast Alaska. Credit: Vizsla Copper.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 7, 2026
Vizsla Copper (TSXV: VCU; US-OTC: VCUFF) says new drilling at its Palmer copper-zinc project in southeast Alaska highlights the property’s potential for high-grade silver mineralization.
Standout hole CMR26-215 at the AG deposit cut 21 metres grading 4.79% zinc, 0.14% copper, 116.9 grams silver per tonne and 0.27 gram gold from 180.3 metres depth, Vizsla Copper said Wednesday . Within that interval, a higher-grade section of 7 metres returned 5.46% zinc, 0.17% copper, 207.5 grams silver and 0.45 gram gold from 182 metres downhole.
Located near the Canadian border, about 60 km from tidewater, Palmer is a volcanogenic massive sulphide project that covers about 330 sq. km. The site, which Vizsla Copper acquired in December 2025, has benefited from more than $116 million (C$164 million) of historical investment and roughly 96,000 metres of drilling.
“The AG deposit is an important part of the existing Palmer resource, and these latest results provide additional confidence in the strength and continuity of the mineralization across the central portion of the deposit,” CEO Craig Parry said in a statement.
Resource update
With all three drill holes from the 2026 infill program at AG now complete, Vizsla Copper plans to use the new results to refine its geological model and to work toward an updated mineral resource estimate for Palmer in next year’s first quarter.
Other results released Wednesday included hole CMR26-211, which cut 37.2 metres grading 3.62% zinc, 0.16% copper, 26.1 grams silver and 0.21 grams gold from 145.1 metres depth. This included 12.8 metres of 7.79% zinc, 0.31% copper, 31.7 grams silver and 0.19 grams gold from 169.5 metres downhole.
Vizsla Copper has been expanding its exploration program after drilling earlier this year identified high-grade mineralization in Zone 1 and new mineralization at the HG prospect. Its 2026 drill program is aimed at both expanding known resources and testing new targets across the Palmer district.
The recently completed drilling at AG was the first to take place at the deposit since 2019.
Polymetallic system
Palmer holds 4.77 million indicated tonnes grading 1.69% copper, 5.17% zinc, 0.14% lead, 28.4 grams silver, 0.29 gram gold and 20.6% barite, according to a 2025 resource . That translates into 178 million lb. copper, 543 million lb. zinc, 14.2 million lb. lead, 4.35 million oz. silver, 43,900 oz. gold and 980,400 tonnes barite.
Inferred resources are estimated at 12 million tonnes grading 0.57% copper, 3.92% zinc, 0.47% lead, 66.3 grams silver, 0.33 gram gold and 25.5% barite for 151.5 million lb. copper, 1.04 billion lb. zinc, 125.2 million lb. lead, 25.6 million oz. silver, 128,100 oz. gold and 3.1 million tonnes barite.
AG, which is particularly rich in silver, makes up a significant portion of the site’s inferred resource.
The company has yet to publish an economic study, cost estimate or development schedule for Palmer.
Vizsla Copper shares dropped 5.1% to C$1.11 Wednesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$100 million ($70 million). The stock has traded between 94¢ and C$2.68 in the past year.

Rivian is rolling out Pet Cam, a new feature in software update 2026.36 that lets R2 owners check on a pet left in the vehicle through a live video feed in the Rivian app.
It’s exclusive to the R2. R1T and R1S owners get new remote Pet Mode controls instead, and the same update brings the Rivian Assistant to the R2, four months after the SUV launched.
How Pet Cam works on the R2
Rivian announced the feature today . Pet Cam uses the R2’s interior cabin camera, which the company describes as a “high-definition RGB” unit, to send a full-color view of the cabin to your phone.
The Rivian R2. Pet Cam relies on its color cabin camera. Source: Rivian
There are two ways to use it. You can open a live stream from the Gear Guard section of the Rivian app, with a badge on the video showing the current cabin temperature. Or you can skip the stream entirely, because the app dashboard and your phone’s lock screen get fresh still images of the cabin on a regular basis.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Pet Cam sits in the Gear Guard tile of the Rivian app. Source: Rivian
Most of the time, you don’t want to watch your dog sleep for five minutes. You want a two-second look to confirm everything is fine, and a lock screen snapshot with the temperature on it does that without opening anything.
Rivian also built in an off switch. Anyone sitting in the vehicle can end the live stream with one tap on the center display.
The automaker says more than 60% of its owners travel with a dog, which explains why this got done four months into the R2’s life.
Rivian says more than 60% of its owners travel with a dog. Source: Rivian
R1T and R1S get app controls, no camera
R1 owners aren’t getting Pet Cam. Rivian ties the feature to the R2’s cabin camera and didn’t announce a version for its flagship truck and SUV.
What Gen 1 and Gen 2 R1 owners do get is remote control of Pet Mode, which the R2 gets too. Until now, you had to turn Pet Mode on before you left the vehicle. With 2026.36, you can switch it on from the Rivian app after you’ve walked away, and switch it off by tapping the paw icon in the app’s climate controls.
Either way, the app asks you to confirm first. That’s there so you don’t shut off the climate control by accident, or leave it running for hours.
Pet Mode on the R2’s center display. Source: Rivian
The catch is Connect+
Rivian’s announcement doesn’t mention pricing. But there’s a catch.
Rivian’s own Connect+ page lists “remote camera livestreaming” as a paid feature, not a standard one. Connect+ costs $14.99 a month or $149.99 a year.
The fine print on that page also caps Gear Guard Live Cam at one hour of streaming per day. It says interior viewing only works with Pet Mode enabled and “is not to be used for people.”
Tesla owners will find all of this familiar. Tesla launched Dog Mode in 2019 , and its owner’s manual says you can view the cabin from the Tesla app while the mode is on, with periodic cabin snapshots on newer iPhones. Tesla’s remote live camera view launched as a Premium Connectivity feature , and that plan costs $9.99 a month.
Rivian Assistant reaches the R2
Update 2026.36 also brings Rivian’s AI voice assistant to the R2. It can adjust climate, media and navigation, answer general questions, pull up the weather at your destination, and identify the song that’s playing.
You call it up by pressing the right Haptic Halo Wheel on the steering wheel, tapping an icon on the display, or saying “Hey, Rivian.”
Rivian Assistant on the R2’s center display. Source: Rivian
R1 owners have had it since May. When Rivian launched the “Hey Rivian” assistant , we reported that it would be on the R2 when customer deliveries started. The R2 launched on June 9 , so buyers waited four months for a feature that was supposed to be there on day one. And it needs Connect+ too.
Rivian says 2026.36 is starting to roll out now to eligible R1 and R2 vehicles. It comes a month after RivianOS 2 put the R1 and R2 on one software stack .

If you’ve ever looked at a cargo e-bike and thought, “Sure, but where am I supposed to put the other six people?”, SixThreeZero may finally have the answer.
The company’s latest addition to its growing e-bike and e-trike lineup, the Long Range Luxury Rickshaw , is already a fairly ridiculous machine in its standard form. It combines three wheels, dual motors, rear passenger seating bench, and enough battery capacity to make many electric motorcycles jealous. But start adding its optional passenger trailers, and you can essentially build yourself a seven-person electric bicycle train.
And somehow, that’s still not the craziest number on the spec sheet.
The rickshaw packs a whopping 7,300 Wh of battery capacity. That’s not a typo. We didn’t move a decimal. It’s literally got 10x the battery capacity of most e-bikes.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The setup includes two 48V 20Ah batteries integrated into the frame, plus an enormous 48V 112Ah battery mounted beneath the rear passenger seat. Combined, that works out to 7,296 Wh of capacity.
For comparison, a typical commuter e-bike might have a 500-750 Wh battery.
The company claims up to 120 miles (193 km) of range, though as always, actual range will depend heavily on speed, terrain, assist level, and – perhaps more than with most e-bikes – how many friends you’ve talked into joining your bicycle conga line.
But with that mileage figure working out to an efficiency of around 60 Wh/mi (36 Wh/km), that spec sheet range number might actually be a fairly realistic rating. There are a lot of e-bike companies trying to claim 100-mile ranges with a 720 Wh battery, though they admittedly don’t have the rolling resistance of this e-trike locomotive.
Power comes from a pair of 750W motors. Riders can select single or dual-motor operation, with the latter offering 1,500W of combined nominal power for hills and heavy loads. Top speed is listed at 20 mph (32 km/h), available through either pedal assist or throttle.
The base rickshaw seats the rider plus two rear passengers and starts at a rather hefty $7,495 . But that’s where things get interesting.
SixThreeZero offers $999 rear “sub-frames” that attach behind the trike, with options for passenger seating or cargo baskets. Up to two can apparently be connected, creating the seven-person configuration pictured above.
There are even powered versions of those sub-frames with their own motor and battery, controlled from the cockpit of the main bike. At that point, we’re getting dangerously close to building a Mad Max electric road train one bicycle component at a time.
Other equipment includes hydraulic disc brakes on all three wheels, a torque sensor, 20 x 4-inch fat tires, suspension fork, ergonomic handlebars, headlights with high and low beams, turn signals, mirrors, brake lights, a rear differential, and a front cargo basket.
Oh, and a captain’s chair that looks significantly better than the seats in my first car.
Electrek’s Take
Is a $7,495 three-wheeled e-bike with more than 7 kWh of batteries and a pair of passenger trailers excessive? Absolutely.
But I’m also having trouble pretending I don’t want to load six friends aboard and find out just how far this wonderfully absurd contraption can actually go.
And having personally tested SixThreeZero Rickshaws in the past , including putting at least six people on one (pictured below), I know they make these things well.
Lord help the first guy who ever tries to back one of these e-bike trains up, though.
Definitely don’t try this at home. But if you do, follow my lead and use borrowed kids from around the neighborhood

Tesla delivered just 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3 2026, down 48% from a year ago and the lowest total for the category since 2021. With the Model S and Model X out of production, almost all of them were Cybertrucks.
That gives us the cleanest look yet at Cybertruck sales. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 of the trucks last quarter, a pace of about 30,000 a year from a line it planned for 250,000.
“Other Models” hit a five-year low
Tesla doesn’t report Cybertruck sales. Since the truck launched, Tesla has lumped it into “Other Models” with the Model S, the Model X, and now the Semi and Cybercab, although it’s still unclear how Tesla accounts for deliveries of the latter since it delivers them to itself.
That category came in at 8,295 deliveries in Q3 , according to Tesla’s production and delivery report . It was 15,933 a year ago and 12,364 last quarter.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The last time the number was this low was Q2 2021, when Tesla delivered 1,890 Model S and Model X while it switched both to their refreshed versions.
Production fell too. Tesla built 7,004 “Other Models” in Q3, down 40% from 11,624 a year ago.
Most of that drop is the Model S and Model X disappearing. Production of both ended in April , with about 600 cars left in inventory and a final run of 350 Signature cars still to deliver. They padded “Other Models” for years.
Our estimate: 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks
Three things are left in “Other Models” deliveries: the Cybertruck, the Semi, and leftover Model S and Model X.
The leftovers are small. Between the last inventory cars and the Signature run, we’re talking about a few hundred deliveries at most in Q3.
The Semi is small too. For now. Tesla has been building trucks at its new Nevada factory since April, but it only announced volume production and the start of customer deliveries on September 25 , five days before the quarter ended. In July, Tesla’s own shareholder letter still listed the plant as “commissioning.” We’d put Q3 Semi deliveries in the hundreds.
The Cybercab is the bigger unknown. Tesla clearly produced a few thousand of them, but it’s unclear if it counts any of the few in its robotaxi fleet as “delivered.”
Here’s the math:
Q3 2026 deliveries | Units
“Other Models” (reported by Tesla) | 8,295
Model S and Model X leftovers (Electrek estimate) | a few hundred
Semi (Electrek estimate) | a few hundred
Cybertruck (Electrek estimate) | 7,000 to 8,000
Production is harder to read. Again, Tesla doesn’t say if the 7,004 “other Models” it built include the Cybercab, which went into production at Gigafactory Texas in April. If they do, Tesla built far fewer Cybertrucks than it delivered and sold the rest out of inventory.
A good quarter for the Cybertruck is still a fraction of the plan
By Cybertruck standards, 7,000 to 8,000 is a good quarter.
Using the same math, we estimated about 5,000 Cybertruck deliveries in Q2 2025 and about 21,500 for all of 2025. Cox Automotive’s US estimates are lower still:
Quarter | “Other Models” deliveries (Tesla, global) | Cybertruck sales (Cox, US)
Q3 2024 | 22,915 | 14,416
Q4 2024 | 23,640 | 12,991
Q1 2025 | 12,881 | 6,406
Q2 2025 | 10,394 | 4,306
Q3 2025 | 15,933 | 5,385
Q4 2025 | 11,642 | 4,140
Q1 2026 | 16,130 | 3,519
Q2 2026 | 12,364 | 3,744
Q3 2026 | 8,295 | not out yet
Cox’s numbers have run low before. S&P Global Mobility counted 7,071 Cybertruck registrations in Q4 2025, and 1,339 of those went to SpaceX and Elon Musk’s other companies .
A few things helped in Q3. The cheaper dual-motor trim started reaching customers in late June, and high gas prices have lifted EV demand across the board.
Tesla also had a backlog. When it sued its Cybertruck casting supplier in July , it told the court it had “several thousand Cybertrucks already committed to customers” that it couldn’t build without its tooling. That fight disrupted production for weeks, so some Q3 deliveries were orders Tesla would’ve filled earlier.
Then Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by $5,000 in August . The dual-motor now starts at $74,990.
But even at the top of our range, 8,000 trucks a quarter is 32,000 a year. Tesla planned the Cybertruck line for 250,000 a year, and its latest shareholder letter lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. That’s 13% of the plan and about a quarter of what’s installed.
The Cybertruck is still the best-selling electric pickup in the US, for what that’s worth. Cox had it at 3,744 units in Q2, ahead of the discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning at 2,421, the Chevy Silverado EV at 2,266, and the Rivian R1T at 1,219.

For almost three years, Tesla hid the Cybertruck behind the Model S and Model X. That cover is now mostly gone. Q3 2026 is the first quarter where “Other Models” is basically a Cybertruck number, and it’s 8,295 at the very most.
If Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks, that’s up from where the truck was in 2025. But it took a cheaper trim and a gas price crisis to get there, and Tesla’s response was to raise prices by $5,000. We’ll see what Q4 looks like without the backlog.
However, we don’t expect this clean-er look to last. The Semi is ramping at a factory Tesla says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and every one of them will land in “Other Models.” Within a few quarters, Tesla will be able to point to growth in the category, and the Cybertruck will be hidden again.

Yellow Corp. Teamsters will receive some WARN Act money even though two separate courts found the company was not liable for failing to give 60 days’ advance notice as required by federal law ahead of its July 2023 shutdown .
A Tuesday memo from a Teamsters director to Yellow Corp. local unions said the IBT had reached a settlement in principle with the bankrupt estate allowing the additional claims. The plan includes approximately $17.2 million in claims pertaining to the WARN Act. The deal represents five days of damages under the federal law, with employees falling under the New Jersey WARN Act receiving 30 days of damages.
The agreement also calls for the allowance of $1.2 million in grievance claims that were pending when the company shut down, and $1.8 million in claims for unused personal holidays for New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Western Teamsters that are allowed per their contracts.
The memo also reiterated a prior agreement in which the estate will pay employee claims totaling $71.5 million for paid time off, sick leave and other claims.
“The Teamsters leadership chose full payment on contract claims and some recovery on the WARN Act over years of additional litigation on the WARN Act claims with an uncertain outcome,” the memo said.
The deal still has to be signed by both parties and approved by a federal bankruptcy court in Delaware. However, the memo said no further objections are expected, noting that Yellow’s largest shareholder, MFN Partners, has withdrawn its objection to a bankruptcy plan confirmation.
Teamsters that were employed by Yellow are expected to receive full payment on their PTO and sick-time claims. A per-person cap of $22,650 is in place ($15,150 for priority claims and $7,500 for additional benefit claims). The memo noted that a few employees have claims exceeding the cap amount and that excess amounts will be paid at the same rate as general unsecured claims, which is projected to be less than 20%.
Payments are expected to be distributed “within months” of the court’s approval, assuming no further appeals.
Yellow terminated 3,500 nonunion employees on July 28, 2023, and 22,000 union employees two days later. The company filed for bankruptcy on Aug. 6, 2023.
The bankruptcy court previously determined that Yellow was a “liquidating fiduciary” winding down affairs, not an operating business, at the time of the layoffs, thus exempt from WARN Act requirements. That decision also said Yellow appeared to act in good faith, but that if the court was found incorrect on its view of the WARN requirements, back pay and benefits should be limited to just 14 days, not the 60 days requested.
The U.S. District Court in Delaware later affirmed the bankruptcy court’s finding, adding that the company also qualified under a separate exemption as a faltering company.
Why it matters? Former employees have some clarity on their financial recovery, which now includes reduced WARN Act payments. Full payment of accrued PTO and sick leave will be distributed within months of the bankruptcy court granting final approval.

Forwarders shipping flowers, pharmaceuticals and other sensitive cargo are being offered a tracking and insurance package combining fixed payouts for qualifying delays with cover for temperature-related losses.
Airfreight wholesaler Solent Freight Services, technology provider Tag-N-Trac and insurance specialist Otonomi have launched TRACinSURED, bringing shipment monitoring and insurance into a single subscription product.
For a flower shipment from Ecuador, a forwarder would enrol the consignment by assigning its airway bill to the system, receiving confirmation once insurance was bound.
“As an illustrative figure for the trial programme, the current pricing discussed is approximately $100 for $2,500 of insured value, including the data logger,” Solent chief marketing officer Nataliya Zagorodnova told The Loadstar .
Final commercial pricing and the trigger schedule are still being approved but customers will be offered monthly and annual subscriptions, with tracking available from airport to door or door to door.
Ms Zagorodnova said the package’s principal advantage was bringing visibility and protection together.
“It is therefore less about simply offering a cheaper version of conventional cargo insurance and more about providing a new type of bundled risk-management product,” she said.
The package combines two different insurance mechanisms. Delay cover is parametric: a defined event triggers a pre-agreed payout, without requiring the customer to demonstrate the extent of physical damage to the goods. Solent said the current structure included six- and 12-hour delay thresholds.
Temperature excursion cover, however, is non-parametric and requires proof of loss, with the sensor record supporting the claim.
Tag-N-Trac’s smart labels and trackers monitor location, temperature, humidity, shock, light and tampering at item, carton or pallet level.
“Solent has spent more than 30 years handling fresh-cut flowers, fruits, pharmaceuticals and other highly perishable cargo where temperature, timing and visibility can determine whether a shipment succeeds or fails,” said chief executive Simon Milne.
“For years, we – along with the transportation industry worldwide – have been looking for a way to bring shipment tracking, temperature monitoring and delay protection together in one simple, powerful package.”
Otonomi designs and administers the insurance. Ms Zagorodnova said it was underwritten through Lloyd’s.
The partners say qualifying parametric claims can typically be settled within days. Payouts are agreed in advance and may differ from the actual loss.
The product is also intended for use beyond Solent’s own freight network.
“Solent’s role is not to become the operational carrier for every insured shipment,” Ms Zagorodnova explained. “The freight forwarder remains responsible for operating the shipment; TRACinSURED provides the tracking and insurance solution.”
However, shipment visibility does not come with an automatic intervention service.
“Customers should not assume that every alert automatically triggers corrective action, rerouting or other physical intervention,” she said. “Operational decisions remain with the freight forwarder or logistics operator handling the shipment.”
Solent is targeting global distribution, with active countries, lanes and underwriting arrangements subject to confirmation during the rollout.
The launch programme includes an introduction at Ecuador’s flower show on 6–8 October, followed by a fuller launch at TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami later this month.

source_document.body:
An M1A2 Abrams main battle tank with 1-16th Infantry, 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Infantry Division, conducts a Live Fire Accuracy Screening Test Sept. 28, 2025, on Novo Selo Training Area, Bulgaria. (U.S. Army photo by Spc. Brandi Frizzell)
WASHINGTON — General Dynamics Land Systems has partnered with Primordial Labs to bring AI voice-control to its combat vehicles, ranging from the iconic M1 tank to the next-gen XM30, the companie s plan to an nounce later this morning.
Coming jus t days ahead of the massive annual AUSA trade shadow in DC, this odd couple combines a classic heavy-metal military manufacturer, which has built the M1 for over 40 years , with a young AI startup best known for demonstrations with small drones.
But Primordial built its Anura voice-control system to be platform-agnostic — it’s also working on AI assistance for Army helicopter crews — and adaptable to any kind of vehicle, co-founder Lee Ritholz told Breaking Defense. “We’re [used to] doing everything on a really tiny processor,” he said. “As we get to these larger platforms, it becomes almost a luxury” by comparison.
GDLS, for its part, sees tremendous potential for voice control to help increasingly overburdened human soldiers manage an ever-growing array of complex systems, from tactical data networks to AI target recognition , company officials said in interviews.
“There’s a bunch of technology being thrown at soldiers,” explained Salem Auclair, a 20-year Army veteran who helped write the official requirements for the XM30 before joining Primordial. The XM30 program, for which GDLS is competing with American Rheinmetall , actually calls for shrinking the crew from three soldiers on today’s M2 Bradley to two on XM30, while adding more technology.
“These are the same 18- to 22-year-old soldiers that that are driving these vehicles now, and we’re giving them more complex system,” Auclair said. “Well, how can we help them use those systems? Give them a mechanism that they’re used to, their voice.”
Geoff Norman, GDLS’s director of strategy and a retired Army general who worked on the next-gen vehicle program, said, “having to flip switches and push buttons and type on keyboards and do the manual tasks in a combat vehicle, on the move, in the dark, in bad weather … will be a challenge in the future, especially given that those tasks are going to be done by a smaller crew.”
With AI voice control, by contrast, a soldier just needs to give a verbal order, and the software should be smart enough to take care of the rest, the two companies’ experts explained. In many ways, Anu ra is designed to act as an additional, virtual crew member, to which the human soldiers can delegate a wide range of tasks — especially time-consuming or technically complex ones — so they can stay focused on the fight. Company officials said it can even help manage other automated systems, for example by telling an AI threat-detection system to scan for flank attacks while the humans focus a target up ahead.
However, Anura won’t be able to fire a vehicle’s weapons, the companies emphasized.
“We’re not talking to the fire control system and doing … lethality tasks,” Norman said. “What we’ve chosen are things like doing communications, adjusting which radio net you’re on, sending reports that otherwise you would have to type in, adjusting the camera view that you’re looking out of the vehicle on. Those things are easy to verify and validate for a safety case.”
Anura isn’t using generative AI, the kind of superpowered but unpredictable chatbot that has roiled the world since the launch of ChatGPT.
“We can’t hallucinate because we don’t generate things,” Ritholtz said. “We’re not using generative AI.”
Instead, he explained, Anura uses more narrowly focused and predictable forms of machine learning, which in turn serve as translators between the human soldier’s voice commands and the complex, often user-unfriendly interfaces of military systems.
Anura isn’t installed on the current XM30 prototypes now in testing by the Army, Norman said, but GDLS aims to offer it on future upgrades, both to XM30 and to legacy vehicles like the M1 tank and Stryker troop carrier.

source_document.body:
Porsche Boxster EV charging at Tesla Supercharger in California. Photo: Roland J, used with permission
Porsche has finally confirmed that there will be no more gas-powered Boxster/Cayman going forward, and that all-electric versions of those vehicles will have their first production year in 2028.
The move shows that Porsche is finally ready to bring electric power to its sportscars… but Porsche’s CEO still says the 911 will “never” go electric. We think time will show him to be wrong on that one.
Porsche held an investor presentation today, laying out its strategy through 2035.
In it, it talked about the future of the 718, otherwise known as the Boxster convertible and Cayman hardtop.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The gas-powered versions of these two vehicles went out of production in 2025, and since then, there have been rumors swirling about which direction Porsche would go with the model going forward: gas or electric.
Most of the rumors assumed that the next model would be electric, but some holdouts who just can’t give up their bad powertrain were trying to manifest a return of a gas engine.
But thankfully for everyone who either enjoys driving responsive vehicles or breathing air, Porsche has now put the kibosh on that, and says that going forward the 718 is going to be solely battery powered.
In the company’s presentation, the 718 was listed as a solely electric model, with 2028 being its “first full year of production.”
And the news about the car went further, as Car and Driver got a chance to go for a ride-along in it around Porsche’s Weissach test track.
Porsche 718 has mid-mounted battery to retain handling characteristics
This included the reveal of one aspect of the car we hadn’t yet heard about – its battery configuration.
Most EVs these days have the battery low-slung at the bottom of the vehicle, which helps cornering by lowering the car’s center of gravity. This reduces roll and makes the car feel more stable and planted when turning.
But it also raises the seating position, making the driver feel a little further from the road. For a sportscar, sitting low is part of the feel of driving, so it’s a bit of a compromise in that respect.
So the 718 actually mounts the battery behind the seats, rather than underneath them. This allows for a lower seating position, and also allows for a dynamic balance more similar to the outgoing mid-engined gas versions, which have their engine positioned behind the seats as well. The gas Boxster had a 59.8% rear weight bias, while the EV has 55.2% rear.
Car and Driver called this configuration “unique,” but… it isn’t really. In fact, the very first EV of the modern age, the Tesla Roadster, has a similar battery configuration. In practice (and I have a lot of practice, I own one), this gives a rear-wheel drive vehicle like the 718 or the Roadster incredible traction under acceleration, as so much of the car’s weight is over the drive wheels. (The Roadster was even more rear-weight-biased, with roughly 35/65 front-rear distribution)
Porsche CEO says the 911 will ‘never’ go electric… but we’re not so sure about that
The commitment to an electric 718 is significant, given that Porsche has been back and forth on electrification.
The company recently booked a $6 billion loss due to its EV intransigence , and pivoted back towards combustion engines despite the fact that its main problems have been in markets where’s its sales are being siphoned away by electric rivals from China.
So we’re glad to see them committing to an electric 718, though perhaps less glad to hear about an upcoming new SUV which will be gas and plug-in hybrid, a silly decision in a world where the downsides of oil are so readily apparent .
But now that Porsche has committed on the 718, the question then comes of when it will electrify its iconic 911.
The 911 has served as the brand’s signature for more than half a century, continually produced and modified since then. And it has been a popular vehicle for enthusiasts and a halo car for the Porsche brand all along.
And now we have an answer: during the presentation, Porsche CEO Michael Leiters said “the 911 will never be electric.”
That certainly puts a pin on it, and seems to answer the question for good. But we’re not so sure about that.
Yes, the Porsche 911 will go electric
“Never” is a long time, even for Porsche’s famously stubborn fanbase. Yes, Porsche fans complain any time the company improves their cars – they complained when it started using water cooling for engines, they complained when it started using electric power steering. And they’ll complain when Porsche electrifies the 911.
Why do we think Porsche will electrify the 911? Because Porsche will electrify everything. So will everyone else.
There are two options for the future of this planet: In the long term, humanity either stops extracting oil from the Earth to turn into gasoline and burn in car engines, or human civilization no longer has the level of organization required to support a luxury automaker like Porsche.
We all know this, and we are currently seeing the clear effects of how horrible this oil addiction is for everyone. Countries, companies and drivers are rapidly getting their act together and trying to electrify as quickly as possible. The companies and countries that are providing for that electrification are seeing great success .
This will, in the medium and long term, be accompanied by a collapse of everything to do with oil and oil-powered vehicles .
So imagine, 20 years from now, when Porsche is no longer able to sell gas-powered 911s in Europe , in China , or in its major US markets . Will the Porsche still “never” be electric then? Where are you going to sell those cars? Laos ? Ethiopia ? Nepal ?
Porsche will electrify the 911 if it wants to win races
And even if you don’t acknowledge the inevitable scientific realities of the previous few paragraphs, all you need to do is look at recent racing results to see the way the arrow is moving.
Xiaomi, a smartphone-maker with no experience building cars, built an EV and had beaten Porsche at Porsche’s own playground only about three years after the company first put pen to paper. The record has since traded back to Porsche , but this and other impressive EV racing results show that EVs are just getting better.
If the 911 is Porsche’s halo car, the car that brings people into the brand, the car that Porsche uses to dominate racing, how is that going to look in a decade or two when anyone can slap together a performance EV and stomp a gas-powered competitor, no matter how much “racing heritage” the latter has?
Will Porsche start marketing the 911 as a return to a bygone era, having the same success as horse-and-buggy companies in the 1950s? Will Porsche drop the brand that it has maintained and that has led its company’s sales for decades, out of some ridiculous sense of “purity” for the 911 that must remain unsullied by a superior powertrain? Or will Porsche do the obvious thing and swap to a better powertrain to provide a better vehicle?
So, we disagree with Leiters here. The 911 will (not “should”) eventually become electric. Either that, or the 911 or Porsche will cease to exist. There’s no other option.

Kia EV2 sees strong demand after launch
Kia’s smallest electric SUV is off to a promising start. After opening orders in Europe and the UK in April, Kia sold over 8,000 EV2s in its first full three months on the market.
With deliveries now in full swing, the EV2 helped propel Kia to its highest-ever third-quarter sales since it began selling vehicles in 1962.
Kia is now the fastest-growing top 10 car brand in Europe, thanks to its full lineup of electric vehicles ranging from the entry-level EV2 to the three-row EV9 and PV5 van.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
After EV registrations surged 58% year-on-year through August, Kia accounted for 4.8% of the European EV market, ranking seventh overall. In markets like France (+120%), Germany (+112%), the UK (+66%), Spain (+60%), and Italy (+41%), Kia saw particularly strong demand.
Kia EV2 GT-Line S (Source: Kia UK)
The EV3 remained among Kia’s most popular EVs, while newer models like the EV2, EV4, and EV5 also helped drive growth.
In the UK, a key battleground market, Kia said the EV2, which only began full-scale customer deliveries in mid-Q3, “saw significant and immediate demand” from buyers. The EV2 has managed 3,386 registrations year-to-date (YTD), with 1,753 in September alone.
From left to right: Kia EV2, EV3, EV5, and EV9 (Source: Kia UK)
According to Kia, the EV2 was “the UK’s most popular retail-market EV” with 1,429 registrations in September.
Kia has delivered 31,813 electric vehicles in the UK YTD, accounting for more than 33% of its total registrations. Behind Tesla, Kia is now the UK’s second best-selling electric car brand through September.
Kia EV2 interior UK (Source: Kia UK)
The EV2 Air long edition is on sale starting at £24,245 ($32,500) in the UK, including the government’s £3,750 Electric Clean Car Grant (ECG).
It’s available in four trims: Light, Air, Earth, and GT-Line. Buyers can choose from two battery packs: 42.2 kWh and 61 kWh, providing WLTP ranges of up to 317 km (197 miles) and 453 km (281 miles), respectively.

The PV5 Cargo, Kia’s electric work van, is also the UK’s best-selling small electric commercial vehicle (E-LCV), with 4,654 registrations YTD.
Meanwhile, the PV5 Passenger was the most popular “van-derived car” in September with 390 registrations. Kia has delivered 1,704 PV5 Passenger models YTD.
While the US will miss out on the EV2 and PV5, the 2027 EV3 ( check out our review ) is now on sale, starting at about $30,000. In its first full month of sales, Kia sold just over 500 EV3s in the US. Kia is now on pace for a fourth consecutive record year of sales in the US.
